One of the best Japanese denim overviews yet, and includes a lot of details most miss or misrepresent. There is one major omission though, you didn't cover dyeing! Japanese denim almost entirely uses rope-dyed indigo, usually synthetic but sometimes natural indigo. Indigo has a different chemistry to most mass produced reactive dyed jeans, in that it has a weaker bond to the cotton and comes off easier. Rope-dyeing the yarns ensure the dye also doesnt penetrate to the core. It makes jeans deliberately designed to fade and age beautifully.

I noticed you didnt mention that selvedge denim is fairly wasteful, because the outseam must be cut on the selvedge edge. They arent woven in the shape of a pant leg, so anything in the center is essentially waste material (or just used for waist bands/pockets/button bands). I think its important. As long as the grain line follows the warp you're getting the strongest orientation for your cut. The selvedge edge is fun for how it looks, but if youre not actually working in them it doesnt really matter as long as your clothes are cut on grain.

The exactness is something that plagues us in the cigarette manufacturing industry. If the cellophane isn’t exactly folded by the machine (Focke 750) or the foil isn’t exactly as they want (Focke 550) they will return the product. The Japanese market exemplifies the perfect being the enemy of the good. It’s still the same cigarette made to the highest standard we can make, If you want every cellophane seal to be within the same millimeter between different batches and from different machines then you will need to go operate those machines yourself. That tolerance doesn’t matter, if we maintained that we would have more downtime than runtime.
